item.content:encoded:
Andrés Giménez is set to return to Toronto's lineup for Saturday's game against the Texas Rangers, batting eighth after missing a pair of contests with hamstring soreness.
The 28-year-old initially exited Tuesday's game against the Detroit Tigers with the injury in the eighth inning before sitting out Wednesday and Friday.
Although he didn't make it into Friday's series opener against the Rangers, Blue Jays manager John Schneider said pre-game that the three-time Gold Glover would have been available off the bench if needed.
He's hitting .243/.288/.359 with nine home runs and 57 RBIs in 140 games this season.
On the defensive side of the ball, Giménez ranks ninth among qualified major-league shortstops with one defensive run saved and second with 19 outs above average.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Mets' Francisco Lindor on 'mentor' Carlos Beltrán and relationship that helped him transition to life in New York
item.dc:creator: Phillip Martinez
item.description: Mets shortstop Francisco Lindor understands how momentous Saturday at Citi Field is. The organization is honoring Carlos Beltrán by inducting him into the Mets Hall of Fame and retiring his No. 15. Beltrán is a player who not only represented the franchise as one of its best players, but as a fellow Puerto Rican, the honor hits close to home for Lindor. "It's very inspiring. Someone that was close to me and to every Puerto Rican. Anybody that's Puerto Rican that makes it big, us Puerto Ricans fe
item.content:encoded:
Mets shortstop Francisco Lindor understands how momentous Saturday at Citi Field is.
The organization is honoring Carlos Beltrán by inducting him into the Mets Hall of Fame and retiring his No. 15. Beltrán is a player who not only represented the franchise as one of its best players, but as a fellow Puerto Rican, the honor hits close to home for Lindor.
"It's very inspiring. Someone that was close to me and to every Puerto Rican. Anybody that's Puerto Rican that makes it big, us Puerto Ricans feel like we made it as well," Lindor said in the clubhouse prior to Saturday's game. "To be on the biggest stages, playoffs, All-Star games and to see him come back to the island is very special. We always talk about guys like that, like the Beltráns, [Roberto] Alomar, [Carlos] Delgado, [Ivan]Rodriguez. Guys that set the path for a guy like me today."
Lindor looked up to Beltrán because he was also a switch-hitter from the island, who played hard and "had swag," but he wouldn't get a chance to build a relationship with one of his idols until 2016.
Lindor, playing with Cleveland at the time, just wrapped up a series with the Beltrán's Yankees right before the All-Star break. The young shortstop was heading to San Diego for his first All-Star Game and shared a plane with the outfielder and a few other Yankees who also made the Midsummer Classic. That's when he had an opportunity to speak with the future Hall of Famer.
"Anybody that's from Puerto Rico and makes it big, us Puerto Ricans feel like we made it, as well."
Francisco Lindor says it was "very inspiring" to see Carlos Beltrán's success in Major League Baseball: pic.twitter.com/5QX8pUuM4n
"He's a mentor. Someone you can have a conversation with him, tell him the stuff I'm going through because he probably already went through it. He's helped me for sure," Lindor said of Beltrán. "I look up to him growing up and to have an opportunity to share the field with him. To have moments to talk to him. It's something I don't take for granted."
That relationship came in handy when Lindor was traded to the Mets in 2021. It was an adjustment period for Lindor, who struggled on and off the field. Going from a small market to New York City was tough for Lindor, but he had Beltrán to help him.
Beltran got Lindor in touch with a realtor and helped him with the off-the-field transition, but also offered a shoulder when the on-the-field production wasn't there.
"When I first got traded here, I called him and I talked to him," Lindor said. "I didn't play well. I sucked in the beginning and having him there to comfort me and say, 'Hey, this stuff is going to happen. It's ok. You're going to go through stuff like this, but you're going to come out on the other side. Stay true to yourself and play the game the right way.'
"Stuff like that early on was huge for me today."
Five years later, and Lindor has become an important part of the team on the field and as a locker room leader.
"I love Francisco. I admire him. I love the way he plays. I always watch the switch-hitters in the game," Beltrán said prior to his number retirement ceremony. "He will be in this position at some point in life. I'm grateful for the friendship that we have...We have a good relationship. We talk about baseball, we talk about hitting, life, family, we talk about kids, we talk about everything.
"The relationship I was able to build with him is a friendship more than anything else."
Could that relationship-building help Beltrán get a managerial job with the Mets or elsewhere? Lindor was asked and the shortstop is convinced the Hall of Famer will succeed in that realm if that's his desire.
"If he wants it. I believe he'll succeed whenever he becomes a manager," Lindor said. "If the organization feels that's the right fit for us…. If he decides to pursue, and if they feel he's the best fit, he'll succeed at it.
"To be a manager is not about respect, it's about knowing the game, making the right moves at the right time and connecting with players. And I think he can do all those."
"I love Francisco. I admire him. I love the way he plays. Being a switch-hitter, I'm always watching the switch-hitters in the game. He will be in this position at some point in life."
- Carlos Beltrán on Francisco Lindor pic.twitter.com/gwQGCW2KP5

item.dc:creator: Justin Binkowski; Unknown

item.content:encoded:
There hasn't been much for New York Mets fans to get excited about in 2026. But on Friday night, Mets outfielder Juan Soto accomplished a feat that only three other superstars have done in MLB history.
Soto launched a 428-foot three-run blast in New York's 6-3 win over the Philadelphia Phillies on Friday. Despite dealing with injuries this season, the lefty-swinging slugger now has 26 home runs in 103 games. This was also the 27-year-old's 270th homer in the majors. That's noteworthy because the five-time All-Star is now one of just four players to reach 270 home runs and 100 stolen bases before their 28th birthday, according to MLB.com's Sarah Langs.
The other stars on this list include Hall of Famer Ken Griffey Jr. and a pair of three-time MVPs in Alex Rodriguez and Mike Trout. All four players in this exclusive group were playing in the big leagues at 19. And with Soto wrapping up just the second season of his 15-year contract with the Mets, New York fans should get to see the talented outfielder make more history for the foreseeable future.
What's next for Juan Soto and the Mets in 2027?
Heading into the 2026 season, several pundits thought the Mets could compete for the top spot in the National League East. Instead, New York is currently in last place in the NL East at 70-84. But it's not all doom and gloom for the Mets beyond this year's campaign.
In addition to Soto continuing to play like a star while healthy, some of New York's talented prospects have emerged as potential key pieces to the team's future. Starting pitcher Nolan McLean and outfielder Carson Benge should receive some National League Rookie of the Year votes this year, and outfielder A.J. Ewing has turned heads by reaching the majors after starting 2026 at Double-A. The Mets also revamped their farm system at the trade deadline, most notably acquiring the team's new No. 1 prospect, infielder Jefferson Rojas.
New York is expected to be a major spender in the offseason as well. Owner Steve Cohen could make an aggressive offer for left-handed ace Tarik Skubal, while also targeting other top free agents. Either way, with the 2026 season almost in the rearview mirror for the Mets, many fans will be waiting to see if the team can bounce back in 2027.
Justin Binkowski is a lifelong baseball fan returning to cover the sport he loves after spending nearly a decade writing about video games. Before his time as managing editor at Dot Esports, Binkowski attended King's College in Wilkes-Barre, PA, where he was also a relief pitcher on the school's baseball team. While in college, Binkowski was a media relations intern for the Scranton/Wilkes-Barre RailRiders during the 2014 season.

item.content:encoded:
Cardinals dejan en libertad al mexicano Ramón Urías a días de terminar la temporada de MLB
St. Louis liberó al infielder sonorense apenas dos días después de designarlo para asignación; el ganador del Guante de Oro queda disponible con poco más de una semana por jugar en la temporada regular.
La etapa de Ramón Urías con los St. Louis Cardinals terminó antes de lo esperado. El equipo dejó oficialmente en libertad al infielder mexicano este viernes 18 de septiembre, cuando resta poco más de una semana para que concluya la temporada regular de MLB 2026.
El movimiento llegó solamente dos días después de que St. Louis designara para asignación al sonorense, el miércoles 16 de septiembre, como parte de los ajustes realizados para reincorporar al infielder JJ Wetherholt desde la lista de lesionados.
Al quedar liberado, Urías vuelve a estar disponible para buscar una oportunidad con otra organización, poniendo fin a una segunda etapa con los Cardinals que duró apenas unos meses.
Ramón Urías había firmado con Cardinals para 2026
St. Louis incorporó a Ramón Urías como agente libre el pasado 21 de febrero, mediante un contrato por una temporada que también contemplaba una opción mutua para 2027.
El movimiento representaba además un regreso a una organización conocida para el mexicano.
Cardinals había adquirido previamente sus derechos procedente de los Diablos Rojos del México en 2018, y Urías pasó dos temporadas dentro de sus sucursales antes de ser designado para asignación en 2020. Posteriormente, Baltimore Orioles lo reclamó de waivers y fue con esa organización donde logró establecerse en las Grandes Ligas.
Seis años después regresó a St. Louis, ahora convertido en un veterano con experiencia en MLB y con un Guante de Oro de la Liga Americana, conseguido como tercera base de Baltimore en 2022.
Sin embargo, su regreso a los Cardinals terminó siendo breve.
Te podría interesar: José Rodríguez rompe una espera de 25 años para Oaxaca con su debut en MLB
Una lesión frenó la temporada del mexicano
Urías tuvo una campaña complicada principalmente por problemas físicos.
El mexicano fue colocado en la lista de lesionados el 5 de mayo debido a una epicondilitis lateral en el codo derecho y posteriormente fue transferido a la lista de 60 días. No regresó al roster activo hasta el 23 de agosto, después de más de tres meses fuera.
La larga ausencia le impidió encontrar continuidad ofensiva.
En 83 turnos al bat durante 2026, Urías registró:
- Promedio: .157
- Hits: 13
- Jonrones: 4
- Carreras producidas: 9
- OPS: .605
Sus números contrastaron con una trayectoria en la que mantiene promedio vitalicio de .253, con 54 cuadrangulares y 224 carreras impulsadas en Grandes Ligas.
Cardinals lo liberan a nueve días del final de temporada
La fecha vuelve particularmente llamativo el movimiento.
La temporada regular de MLB 2026 concluirá el domingo 27 de septiembre, por lo que St. Louis decidió separarse del mexicano apenas nueve días antes del último día del calendario.
Los Cardinals habían designado para asignación tanto a Urías como al pitcher Peter Strzelecki el 16 de septiembre. Dos días más tarde, Strzelecki fue enviado definitivamente a Triple-A Memphis, mientras que Urías fue liberado.
De esta manera, el infielder nacido en Magdalena de Kino, Sonora, queda nuevamente en busca de equipo después de vestir los uniformes de Baltimore Orioles, Houston Astros y St. Louis Cardinals durante su trayectoria en las Grandes Ligas.
A sus 32 años, Urías cuenta además con la ventaja de su versatilidad defensiva: a lo largo de su carrera ha cubierto tercera base, segunda, shortstop y primera base, además de contar con el antecedente de haber sido reconocido como el mejor antesalista defensivo de la Liga Americana en 2022.
Ahora tendrá que esperar para conocer cuál será el siguiente capítulo de su carrera, después de que su regreso a la organización de los Cardinals terminara apenas siete meses después de su firma.

item.content:encoded:
The 2026 season could end up being Sonny Gray’s last.
The veteran right-hander, who turns 37 in November, has not committed to pitching in 2027 and recently told The Boston Globe he would retire “in a heartbeat” if his family wanted him to do so.
Boston reportedly is taking the possibility seriously, according to the outlet, with some in the organization believing retirement is on the table despite Gray’s strong season.
Asked recently about the possibility of retirement, Gray declined to say much.
“We can get into that at another time but not right now,” he said, per the Globe.
If 2026 is, indeed, his final big league season, Gray’s final start could come in the increasingly likely matchup against the rival Yankees during the wild-card round of the postseason.
Gray spent a season and a half in pinstripes after coming over before the 2017 trade deadline, and it didn’t go exactly as planned for either him or the team.
The three-time All-Star posted a 4.51 ERA across 41 games (34 starts) with the Yankees before being traded to Cincinnati before the 2019 season, during which he posted a Cy Young-caliber season with the Reds.
Gray ripped the Yankees during his introductory press conference with the Red Sox over the winter.
“It feels good to me to go to a place where it’s easy to hate the Yankees,” Gray said.
“I never wanted to go there in the first place.”
Gray is enjoying one of the best seasons of his 14-year MLB career in Beantown, posting a 2.82 ERA in 163 innings.
“I’ve very, very much so enjoyed Boston. Enjoyed the guys. Fenway has been, and is, a very special place,” Gray said.

item.content:encoded:
The Toronto Blue Jays dropped their first game against the Texas Rangers. Their 7-1 loss dropped their MLB playoff chances to 14.8 percent. Meanwhile, the team announced personal news about George Springer.
Game 2 of their series against the Rangers is scheduled for 5:05 PM Mountain Time, 7:05 PM Eastern Time on Saturday, September 19th, 2026. Jose Soriano takes the mound for the Blue Jays as Cal Quantrill looks to squash their playoff hopes for good.
Toronto Blue Jays’ George Springer Personal News Emerges During Texas Rangers Series
Before the second game of their series against the Rangers, personal news about the Blue Jays’ Springer emerged.
His MLB profile page shows that Springer’s birthday is September 19th, along with a few other personal details:
- George Chelston Springer
- Nickname: Horhay
- Born: 9/19/1989 in New Britain, CT
- Draft: 2011, Houston Astros, Round: 1, Overall Pick: 11
As of today, Springer is 37 years old.
“A Special Day 4 Springer. Happy Birthday, Georgie,” the team announced on Saturday morning.
George Springer Was Recently Recognized For His Contributions Off The Field
Earlier this week, Springer was the Blue Jays nominee for the Roberto Clemente Award.
MLB.com states that “The Roberto Clemente Award is the annual recognition of a Major League player who best represents the game of baseball through extraordinary character, community involvement, philanthropy, and positive contributions, both on and off the field.”
Springer’s nomination reflects what he has done in the community this year and over the six years he has spent with Toronto.
The award has been around since 1971. It was first called the “Commissioner’s Award.” It was renamed the Roberto Clemente Award in 1973, after Clemente’s tragic passing in 1972.
George Springer’s Future With The Toronto Blue Jays
Springer is on an expiring contract.
The Blue Jays traded Daulton Varsho, Kevin Gausman, and Jeff Hoffman to the Houston Astros, Chicago Cubs, and Minnesota Twins, respectively, at the trade deadline. However, they kept Springer and Shane Bieber.
At the time, it was because keeping Springer gave them the best chance at winning. But will that hold true for next season?
With this season nearly over, and the Blue Jays playoff hopes all but gone, it’s time to take a serious look at if he has a future with the organization.
The Blue Jays are loaded with young talent, and should be leaning into that. This offseason, they might need to make the difficult decision of moving on from Springer, despite everything he has brought to the organization.
After all, Springer isn’t getting any younger.

item.content:encoded:
On Saturday, the San Francisco Giants will continue their series with the Dodgers in Los Angeles.
They are coming off an 8-2 loss on Friday night.
Jack Harris of The California Post wrote: “On the 20th anniversary of the 4+1 game, LAD broke it open tonight with four HRs in the eighth, and five total. Also got 6 IP/2 ER/10 K from Tyler Glasnow, plus a scoreless ninth from Edwin Díaz in his return from IL”
San Francisco Giants Announce Marcelo Mayer Update
Also on Friday, the Giants announced the latest update on Marcelo Mayer.
He has yet to make his debut for the franchise (at the MLB level).
MLB.com wrote (on September 18): “Traveled with the Giants to Los Angeles and ran the bases at Dodger Stadium on Sept. 18.”
According to the site, he could still return before the end of the 2026 regular season.
Alex Pavlovic of NBC Sports Bay Area wrote (on September 7): “Tony Vitello said “there’s a chance” Marcelo Mayer could appear for Giants before end of year. He is getting closer to a rehab assignment, but they’re also less than three weeks from the end of season. Victor Bericoto is feeling good and is close to a rehab assignment.”
Looking At Mayer
Mayer was among the top prospects in all of baseball.
He was picked in the 1st round of the 2021 MLB Draft by the Boston Red Sox.
The 23-year-old played part of two years for the franchise before getting traded to the Giants earlier this year.
MLB.com wrote (on August 3): “Boston Red Sox traded 2B Marcelo Mayer to San Francisco Giants for LHP Erik Miller and CF Carlos Gutierrez.”
Looking At The Giants Right Now
The Giants have had a tough 2026 season.
They are currently the fourth-place team in the National League West with a 64-90 record in 154 games.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Mets’ Juan Soto Makes Baseball History With Trout, Rodriguez, Griffey
item.dc:creator: Billy Heyen
item.description: Juan Soto has joined one of the most impressive four-player clubs in the history of Major League Baseball. Sure, the New York Mets are mired in the midst of a brutally disappointing season, but that didn't stop Soto from a cool accomplishment on Friday night. item.content:encoded:
Juan Soto has joined one of the most impressive four-player clubs in the history of Major League Baseball.
Sure, the New York Mets are mired in the midst of a brutally disappointing season, but that didn't stop Soto from a cool accomplishment on Friday night.
The starting point for the feat was this: Soto launched the 270th home run of his MLB career, a 428-foot blast against the Philadelphia Phillies:
It's a cooler feat than just 270 homers, though.
Juan Soto's New History
Soto has become just the fourth player in major league history with at least 270 home runs and at least 100 stolen bases before turning 28 years old, according to MLB's Sarah Langs.
The other three players on the list:
- Ken Griffey Jr.
No old-timers on the list, but those might be the three best pure baseball players of the last few decades, along with Barry Bonds.
A-Rod, Junior and Trout don't need full names to even be identified.
Soto doesn't quite have that going, although if you start talking about a ballplayer named Soto, people will know who you're referring to.
He's not going to have a postseason audience this season, either. A year ago, the Mets collapsed down the stretch. This season, they were never really in the race.
Soto has had a solid season when healthy — in 103 games, he had 26 home runs and a .920 OPS.
Juan Soto Career Stats
Soto has now played in 1,199 MLB games to reach the 270 home run mark.
He also has 210 doubles as part of 1,187 hits and counting.
Soto has also stolen 104 bases in 134 attempts. The big steals year came last season, when he swiped 38 bags pretty much out of nowhere. His previous career-high had been 12 steals in two separate seasons. In 2026, Soto is 9-for-12 stealing bases.
The lefty Soto is also well-known for his ability to work a walk, and it's pretty much historic. He has led all of MLB in walks in four separate seasons, and he has six years with at least 100 walks.
For his career, Soto has walked 969 times and only struck out 893 times, a feat pretty much no one else these days even comes close to.
Soto is the active leader among MLB players in on-base percentage at .415.
He still has a long time to go on his Mets contract, and it's safe to expect Soto to continue adding to his great statistics en route to what very well could be a Hall of Fame career.
At some point, though, Mets fans are going to want to see Soto's production be a part of a playoff team — that was the plan all along when Steven Cohen started dishing out so much money, and it'll be up to Soto in part to lead a turnaround and make things right again at Citi Field.
This article was originally published on HEAVY
The post Mets' Juan Soto Makes Baseball History With Trout, Rodriguez, Griffey appeared first on HEAVY.

item.content:encoded:
Bryce Harper and his Philadelphia Phillies will square off against the New York Mets at Citi Field, on Saturday, Sept. 19 at 4:10 p.m. ET. Harper has +440 odds to hit a home run as of Saturday morning.
What It Means
Harper is hitting for a .272 BA, .385 OBP and .494 SLG with a 21.8% strikeout rate and a 15.8% walk rate. His OPS is .879, which ranks 10th in MLB, and he has scored 90 runs. In 657 plate appearances, he has hit 28 home runs and driven in 84 runs. In his last game he had a hitless performance (0 for 4) against the Mets.
The Mets will send Christian Scott (4-5) to the mound for his 23rd start of the season. He is 4-5 with a 3.76 ERA and 127 strikeouts through 105 1/3 innings pitched.

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Mariners Face a Leadership Void as Randy Arozarena and J.P. Crawford Near Free Agency
item.dc:creator: Tremayne Person; Unknown
item.description: The Mariners could enter this winter with a different starting shortstop and an opening in left field. Both big shoes to fill along with a much larger hole that would be hard to see on a depth chart. Randy Arozarena is headed toward free agency. J.P. Crawford’s contract also expires after the season. item.content:encoded:
The Mariners could enter this winter with a different starting shortstop and an opening in left field. Both big shoes to fill along with a much larger hole that would be hard to see on a depth chart. Randy Arozarena is headed toward free agency. J.P. Crawford’s contract also expires after the season. It’s likely that the Mariners move on from both, and if they do, the front office will spend plenty of time discussing alignments and where Colt Emerson fits.
They also will need to spend just as much time figuring out who takes over the room. Jon Morosi recently described the 2026 Mariners as the opposite of a cohesive team. We can debate how much clubhouse chemistry matters when the pitching regresses and prominent hitters underperform. Watching this season, it’s obvious Seattle did not look like a group pulling in the same direction.
Mariners Need a Clubhouse Successor Before Opening Day
The Mariners have spent years without steady clubhouse gravity. They’ve continuously churned through veterans. Carlos Santana arrived during the 2022 playoff push. Justin Turner filled the role in 2024. Eugenio Suárez brought his familiar energy back for the 2025 run. They find an established veteran, let him hang around just long enough to settle the room, then they begin their search for the next one.
That routine becomes dangerous when two of the most established players already inside the clubhouse are packing up and walking out together.
Arozarena was Seattle’s lone All-Star in 2026, plays with a pulse and has earned respect by posting up every day. We also watched another layer of his value emerge when Lazaro Montes reached the majors.
Montes spent his first series attached to Arozarena’s hip. There were jokes, celebrations and plenty of dugout energy, but there was also a veteran helping a 21-year-old navigate the largest jump of his career. Arozarena had become a mentor at exactly the moment Seattle’s next wave of young hitters began arriving.
The Mariners can decide his next contract will be too expensive, aging, diminishing defense, or how many outfielders they already have. They still have to replace what walks away with him.
Crawford presents a different version of the same problem. The Mariners have already paid Emerson like a central piece of their future, and the organization views him as Crawford’s successor at shortstop. That makes the transition fairly easy to see. The human transition is something else entirely.
Crawford has been with Seattle since 2019. He’s the longest-tenured Mariner and an established clubhouse leader who has lived through nearly every stage of this organization’s rebuild. He also welcomed Emerson rather than treating the highly paid prospect like an intruder coming after his job.
Emerson can inherit shortstop, but he won’t inherit the seven years of trust Crawford has built in Seattle. Say what you will about Crawford’s defensive lapses; he remains one of the biggest voices in the clubhouse. His name is often one of the first younger players mention when asked who helped them adjust, whether in the field or at the plate. Julio Rodríguez has even gone so far as to say that, among everyone on the roster, Crawford is the teammate he could most easily envision coaching in the majors one day. That’s not empty praise. Crawford carries real influence with his peers, and much of it goes unnoticed outside the clubhouse.
The Mariners will still have prominent voices. Cal Raleigh has become a face of the franchise. Josh Naylor carries himself like a veteran players naturally follow. Julio Rodríguez has reached the point where leadership comes with the size of his contract and stature.
That doesn’t remove Dan Wilson from the conversation, either. If the Mariners already had this many respected players and still struggled to establish a collective identity, the manager owns part of that failure. Adding a ceremonial clubhouse captain will not solve it.
The next veteran has to play and command respect without demanding attention. If they bring in a new face, he’ll have to connect Raleigh, Rodríguez and Naylor with Emerson, Montes, Michael Arroyo and the rest of the young guys arriving behind them.
Re-signing Arozarena would preserve one of those bridges. Bringing Crawford back in a reduced or evolving role could as well. Moving on from both remains a defensible baseball decision, provided the Mariners have an actual succession plan.
We have watched this organization act as though leadership can always be acquired at the last minute or at the trade deadline. The 2026 season exposed the flaw in that thinking.
If Arozarena and Crawford leave, Seattle cannot hand the clubhouse to whoever happens to have the most service time and hope a new identity forms by Opening Day. The Mariners need to know who takes over before the room becomes somebody else’s problem.
Tremayne Person is the Publisher for Mariners On SI and the Site Expert at Friars on Base, with additional bylines across FanSided’s MLB division. He founded the Keep It Electric podcast in 2023 and covers baseball with a blend of analysis, context, and a little well-timed side-eye just to keep things honest. Tremayne grew up a Mariners fan in Richmond, Va., and that passion ultimately led him to move to Seattle to cover the team closely and become a regular at home games. Through his writing, he connects with fans who want a deeper, more personal understanding of the game. When he’s not at T-Mobile Park, he’s with his dog, gaming, or finding the next storyline worth digging into.

item.title: [en.as.com] Dylan Cease said he would “die on the battlefield” for Blue Jays before disastrous start
item.dc:creator: Jennifer Bubel
item.description: Dylan Cease made an emphatic promise to the Toronto Blue Jays before their crucial series against the Texas Rangers, saying he was ready to “die on the battlefield” for his team. The Blue Jays needed Cease to deliver in the opener of a three-game series in Arlington on Friday, with Toronto’s playoff hopes hanging by a thread. Instead, the right-hander endured one of his roughest outings of the season as the Rangers cruised to a 7-1 victory. Dylan Cease pitched 2.2 innings in Texas tonight, his s
item.content:encoded:
Dylan Cease made an emphatic promise to the Toronto Blue Jays before their crucial series against the Texas Rangers, saying he was ready to “die on the battlefield” for his team.
The Blue Jays needed Cease to deliver in the opener of a three-game series in Arlington on Friday, with Toronto’s playoff hopes hanging by a thread. Instead, the right-hander endured one of his roughest outings of the season as the Rangers cruised to a 7-1 victory.
Dylan Cease pitched 2.2 innings in Texas tonight, his shortest outing of the season
He allowed one earned run on three hits and a season-high six walks, but a Blue Jays error resulted in three unearned runs pic.twitter.com/34yYIK4i48
Cease had described the start as the biggest he had made since joining Toronto, although he insisted that he approached it no differently from any other.
“It is, yeah, but right now every single start is just as important as the next,” Cease said before the game. “I treat every single start the same. They all matter the same. Obviously, the stakes are what they are now because we’ve dug ourselves into a little hole, but I don’t treat any start differently.”
The interview was conducted ahead of Friday’s game by Alex Withers on behalf of Casino.org Canada, with the comments made available to AS for use.
Dylan Cease accepted responsibility for Blue Jays’ playoff push
Toronto’s pitching staff has been hit by injuries, increasing the importance of every available starter down the stretch. Cease said he understood the responsibility but didn’t want to allow the playoff pressure to affect his mindset.
“I definitely feel the responsibility, but I wouldn’t say I feel any pressure,” Cease said. “I just want to get the job done and I’m always going to put the effort into it to achieve this. I’m going to die on the battlefield for my team.”
Cease also explained how he tries to turn the pressure of a playoff race into something productive rather than allowing it to become a distraction.
“I care deeply about winning and I want nothing more than to win, but I don’t let it get to a point mentally to where it debilitates me,” he said. “I let it get me to the point where it gives me motivation and focus.”
That mindset was put to the test almost immediately. Cease allowed four runs, three hits, and six walks in just 2⅔ innings against Texas. Only one of the four runs was earned, but the six walks were a season high and Toronto never recovered from an early deficit.
Dylan Cease tonight:
2.2 IP | 3 H | 4 R (1 ER) | 6 BB | 3 K
It's his shortest outing of the season. pic.twitter.com/j3DOvrPbDG
Cease struggled as Blue Jays’ playoff hopes took another hit
The result was damaging because Toronto entered the series already two games behind the Chicago White Sox for the American League’s final wild-card position. The Blue Jays are now 76-78, while the Rangers improved to 77-77 with the victory. Toronto has eight games remaining in the regular season.
Rangers take the lead on sloppy defense by the Blue Jays! Texas and Toronto are both two games back of the final Wild Card spot pic.twitter.com/WGHhPod75Z
— Talkin' Baseball (@TalkinBaseball_) September 19, 2026
Cease had entered Friday’s game with an 11-5 record and a 2.38 ERA according to the statistics available before his start. His season ERA now stands at 2.40 despite the difficult outing.
Before the game, Cease acknowledged the urgency facing Toronto and said the Blue Jays had to maintain their belief that they could still reach the postseason.
“You have to have that mindset. You have to have that belief. It doesn’t pay to be pessimistic,” Cease said. “We’re going out every day and we’re fighting hard.”
He also admitted that Toronto had not been as consistent as they needed to be throughout the season, while arguing that the team had played better baseball during the second half.
“I believe we’ve had a really solid second half,” Cease said. “We’ve genuinely played good baseball, so I think we’re staying level-headed and we know what we’ve got to do.”
Dylan Cease called every game a “must-win”
The Blue Jays still have two games remaining against Texas, but Friday’s loss made their margin for error even smaller.
“Of course, if we win the series it’s going to put us in a way better position than not,” Cease said before the opener. “I truly mean I’m going to treat every single game the same the rest of the way. Every single game that you ever play is a must-win for us.”
Toronto will try to respond Saturday when José Soriano takes the mound against Texas right-hander Cal Quantrill. Soriano entered the game with a 12-7 record and a 3.56 ERA.
Cease’s message before the series was clear. Toronto needed to embrace the pressure, stay focused and fight until the final out.
“I think at this point it’s just laying it all out there and seeing how the chips lie,” he said.
On Friday, though, Toronto’s most important starter lasted just eight outs and the Rangers moved another step closer to the Blue Jays in the playoff race.

item.title: [North Side Baseball] Alex Bregman's Jekyll-and-Hyde Season Hasn't Actually Been That Confusing
item.dc:creator: Randy Holt
item.description: Cubs Video Early season struggles are not necessarily new to Alex Bregman. item.content:encoded:
Cubs Video
Early season struggles are not necessarily new to Alex Bregman. Throughout his career, the season has generally played out in varying levels of fine in the early-going before the production catches fire in July & August. In his first season with the Chicago Cubs, though, things certainly reached a point where we were all left wondering if that typical summer ascent was actually going to manifest.
While Bregman's numbers were otherwise respectable throughout those first three months of the year, he also wasn't providing much in terms of impact. A .243/.343/.347 line kept him close to respectability (97 wRC+), but he also maintained an ISO of only .103 across more than 380 plate appearances. We heard plenty about adjustments being made, but the absence of notable contributions for a player consistently hitting in the two, three, or four holes in the lineup became a glaring shortcoming for the team.
That was particularly true after June. In that month, Bregman slashed just .200/.348/.300 with a 16.5 percent walk rate serving as effectively the one thing keeping him afloat production-wise. Batted ball luck didn't help either, with Bregman going for a BABIP of just .211.
Something happened when the calendar flipped over to July, though.
Bregman has caught fire in a way that very few players throughout the league could match. In roughly 300 plate appearances since July 1, he's at a .291/.368/.598 line with 19 homers, a gaudy .307 ISO, and a 163 wRC+. He's been one of the best hitters the sport has to offer over that stretch, to the point where the whole season numbers land him in fifth among National League position players in fWAR (5.2).
What's even wilder about the turnaround is that there haven't been a whole host of mechanical changes to indicate such a torrid pace since July, which one might typically expect when hearing a term like "adjustments."
Instead, the mechanics have remained steady. Bregman's bat speed and tilt are each identical between his plate appearances into the end of June and the ones that have come since the start of July. His attack angle and attack direction have each shifted by about two degrees, with the swing getting flatter (15 degrees through June 30 vs. 13 degrees since) and favoring a direction closer to center (six degrees through June 30th and four degrees since). It's not a tremendous difference, but one that speaks to his biggest shift (to which we'll get in a moment) on some level. Further, he's moved within the box but only slightly, with each of his depth and distance from the plate increasing by barely more than an inch.
None of these numbers are particularly notable in the grand scheme of things. Had the player been performing at a consistent level throughout the season, we may not have even noticed them at all. Instead, Bregman's shift since his inflection point at the June-July point in the calendar looks to be the result of timing more than anything else.
This is Bregman's swing timing against the three main pitch groups through June 30th:
Bregman was largely in the proper windows against fastballs, but struggles began to present themselves against the other two types. Notably, he was early on off-speed and breaking pitches while some of the contact against breaking pitches specifically spilled toward the end of the bat more frequently than one might like. Which is why it's no surprise that his ability to make quality contact was stifled quite a bit; in April & June, his hard-hit rate against breaking pitches checked in at only 25.9 percent. You're not going to find any level of batted ball luck that way.
Here, however, is Bregman since July 1:
The vertical component of his timing was never really in question against any pitch group. What Bregman has managed to do, though, is rein in the horizontal point of contact and generate swings that are more on time in terms of his bat's placement within the zone upon contact. The two subsequent months saw him increase his rate of hard contact against breaking pitches.
In general, though, this is just a professional hitter doing professional hitter things. At no point this year has Bregman gotten out of his approach or overhauled his mechanics to look for a solution that didn't necessarily need to be found. The approach remained intact and continues to get even better, considering he's walking nearly twice as often this month (11.5 percent) as he's striking out (6.6 percent). This was almost all a matter of timing. It's not purely that—consider the slight change in his bat path—but it's allowed those changes that would otherwise be marginal or entirely unnoticed to actually have some level of impact.
The reality is that we were always going to see this form from Alex Bregman eventually. Maybe not to this extent on the power side of things, but while we may have this perception of two different version of Bregman in 2026, he remains very much the same player he's always been.

item.content:encoded:
Riley Greene News: Pops 21st home run Friday
Greene went 1-for-4 with a walk and a two-run home run in Friday's 11-8 win over the White Sox.
Greene extended his hitting streak to eight games with his 21st home run of the season. He's gone deep twice during the hitting streak while also delivering 10 RBI and a 1.095 OPS. Detroit has a slim chance of making the playoffs with a big surge during the last week of the regular season, and it appears that Greene is going to do his part to help carry the offensive load.

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Yordan Alvarez Reaches 40 Home Runs and Keeps Triple Crown Pursuit Alive
item.dc:creator: Yirsandy Rodriguez; Unknown

item.content:encoded:
Since he hit Seth Lugo’s fastball, Yordan Alvarez knew that ball was out of the park. The hit came off at 107.2 mph and landed 385 feet into right field, right in the second-level seats at Daikin Park to give Houston a 4-1 lead over the Kansas City Royals earlier this week.
Thus continued Alvarez's pursuit of the Triple Crown—the last one was won by Miguel Cabrera in 2012 with the Detroit Tigers in the American League—, hitting his 40th home run of the season to join a select club in the history of the Astros and players born in Cuba.
He became just the fifth player in Astros history to reach that mark:
• Jeff Bagwell — 47 (2000), 43 (1997), 42 (1999)
• Lance Berkman — 45 (2006), 42 (2002)
• Richard Hidalgo — 44 (2000)
• Alex Bregman — 41 (2019)
• Yordan Alvarez — 40 (2026)
The Hall of Fame member, Jeff Bagwell, was the first Houston hitter to hit 40 or more home runs in a season, when he achieved the feat with 43 home runs in 1997, at 29 years old. In his entire career, he finished recording three similar seasons (1997, 1999 and 2000).
The 47 home runs he hit in the 2000 season remained marked as the most in club history. Richard Hidalgo (44 HR in 2000) and Alex Bregman (41 in 2019) have been the youngest hitters to enter the club, both at 25 years old. But this season, he has made the difference in an unprecedented season for a 40-home-run hitter who has worn the Astros uniform, as he leads the league with an offensive line of .311/.429/.598, 1.027 OPS, 189 OPS+, 319 total bases, 103 walks and 32 intentional walks.
After going through a slump in his home run production, with only five in the last 40 games, Alvarez has heated up again with a pair of home runs in his last 10 at-bats, both in the series that Houston won 2-1 against the Royals. Now he is one home run away from tying Tampa Bay Rays third baseman Junior Caminero, who leads the American League with 41, and three RBIs away from reaching Pete Alonso (102).
Houston has eight games remaining to finish the regular season, two more against the Atlanta Braves at home, a two-game road trip against the Seattle Mariners and four against the Athletics.
Another Chapter of Glory Among Cuban Hitters
Alvarez also joined the list of only four Cuban-born hitters who have hit at least 40 home runs in the Majors. The legendary Cooperstown Hall of Fame member, Tony Pérez, was the first Cuban-born hitter to hit at least 40 home runs in a season, when he reached the milestone in the 1970 season with the Cincinnati Reds’ “Big Red Machine.”
Eighteen years later, José Canseco appears on the historical list, at just 23 years old, in his historic 40-40 season (42 home runs and 40 stolen bases), wearing the Oakland Athletics uniform in 1988.
Canseco entered the club four times, repeating the feat with 41 home runs in 1991 and 46 in 1998. Another who reached the milestone was Rafael Palmeiro, who leads the group of Cuban hitters with four 40-home-run seasons (1998-1999 and 2000 and 2002). Seventeen years later, Jorge Soler hit 48 home runs with the Royals and took ownership of the record for Cubans in a single season, leaving behind Palmeiro’s 47-home-run seasons in 1999 and 2001.
For the first time in the club, Alvarez can go much farther if he manages to regain his home run pace in these last nine games. Before reaching the August and September stretch, his worst month in production had been June when he hit six home runs in 26 games. However, as we saw before, he has been able to take only five balls out of the park since August 1 until now, and that has made the race against Caminero become much more attractive.
Alvarez still has the possibility of reaching a Triple Crown by leading all three offensive categories in all of MLB, a feat that no hitter has accomplished since Mickey Mantle with the New York Yankees in 1956 (.353 BA, 52 HR, 130 RBI).

item.content:encoded:
Carroll batted seventh in Friday's game agaisnt the Yankees because of a recent slump, Alex Weiner of Arizona Sports reports.
Carroll, who had a double and two-run home run in a 9-2 loss to New York, entered the contest batting .147 (10-for-68) with a 32.4 strikeout percentage over the previous 19 games. "Corbin's grinding right now. We all know it," manager Torey Lovullo said."Just give him a chance to catch his breath down there, take a little pressure off of him." Carroll hasn't hit lower than fifth this season and never started a game below third in 2025. It's unclear how long Lovullo will keep Carroll this low in the order, but the Diamondbacks are a better team with him in the upper half.

item.title: [The Baltimore Banner] The rookie forever linked to Pete Alonso’s 300th home run celebration
item.dc:creator: Andy Kostka
item.description: Join the dugout. Sign up here for Orioles updates in your inbox. item.content:encoded:
Join the dugout. Sign up here for Orioles updates in your inbox.
In the chaos that follows a momentous occasion such as this, major leaguers turn rowdy and the beer flows, or sprays, all over the walls. On this night, there was plenty of reason to be rowdy. Pete Alonso, the veteran force for the Orioles, joined an exclusive club by hitting his 300th home run.
Naturally, Alonso was thrown into a laundry cart and guided into the showers in the visiting clubhouse at Citi Field in New York. Beers cracked open, clothes became soaked and players hooted and hollered.
But right next to Alonso on Tuesday night, in a separate laundry cart at the eye of the storm, was a rookie reliever sharing in one of Baltimore’s largest celebrations this year. It was Alex Hoppe, the right-hander who arrived in a trade last month, celebrating his first career win.
“Baseball is a beautiful game sometimes,” left-hander Trevor Rogers said.
Long into the future, everyone in that shower-beer-party will remember whom they were celebrating. Alonso’s historic homer, yes. But also a rookie reliever’s first win. They’re at very different points in their careers — one reaching baseball immortality, the other just starting — but all milestones are worth celebrating.
Read More
“It’s such a baseball moment, and that’s why I love this game,” manager Craig Albernaz said. “You can have someone hit their 300th home run and also a reliever getting his first win as a rookie, and they’re both getting beer showers. … That’s what makes baseball great. You have those team moments, and you also recognize the ‘small’ individual accomplishments. Pete’s is big and Hoppe’s is not small, because every accomplishment in this league is big.”
That’s how Hoppe found himself right alongside Alonso with beer spraying all over.
And Alonso’s teammates weren’t surprised to see this slugger share the spotlight. Before they mobbed him, Alonso gave a speech.
“As easy as it can be to get wrapped up in a milestone like that, he talked to us postgame and said it was nothing about him. It was how good we did to come back after being down late,” Rogers said. “That’s the kind of guy he is, the kind of teammate he is. He could’ve not said anything about that. It was his 300th homer. But he’s just a team guy.”
On the field before Friday’s game, Hoppe said all the right things, too. He said the win matters most, and he was probably accurate when he said that in a month no fan will remember it was Hoppe who earned his first win that night.
At the same time, Hoppe will remember it. His family will remember it. Just as for his debut, and for his first save, Hoppe received a baseball from his outing. He also received a memory few people could even imagine.
“I think he can kind of hold that close to him for the rest of his life,” Coby Mayo said. “[Alonso’s] 300th career homer beer shower, and he’s right there alongside with him. Good for Hoppe.”
Hoppe arrived as part of the deal that sent outfielder Taylor Ward to the Seattle Mariners, and he has fit into this quirky bullpen group by following along and not questioning the weird traditions.
The 27-year-old tends to be a quiet figure. He does his work diligently. He chats here and there, but he’s not a boisterous guy like Rece Hinds and Colton Cowser. That is what makes him a fascinating fit for what Hoppe described as an “uncomfortable and cold” but incredible experience alongside Alonso.
Hoppe isn’t surprised, he said, that the Orioles remembered to celebrate him the same way for his first win.
“I think they just wanted another excuse to give another beer shower,” he joked.
But it’s not just that, even if that’s a big part.
“It speaks to the character and the group of guys we have in here,” Hoppe said. “Big accomplishments, small accomplishments, winning is hard and getting these accomplishments are hard and stuff, so it shows the true character of these guys and how we root for each other.”

item.description: AP CINCINNATI (AP) — Jose Trevino lined a two-run single to right field with the bases loaded in the sixth inning and the Cincinnati Reds rallied for a 6-4 victory over the Chicago Cubs on Friday night. Michael Conforto had three hits for the Cubs, who are tied with the Padres and Phillies at 85-69 for the three National League wild cards — five games ahead of Arizona with eight to play. item.content:encoded:
AP
CINCINNATI (AP) — Jose Trevino lined a two-run single to right field with the bases loaded in the sixth inning and the Cincinnati Reds rallied for a 6-4 victory over the Chicago Cubs on Friday night.
Michael Conforto had three hits for the Cubs, who are tied with the Padres and Phillies at 85-69 for the three National League wild cards — five games ahead of Arizona with eight to play.
Chicago had the potential tying run at the plate with two outs in the ninth when Michael Busch was caught stealing second base by Trevino on a pitchout.
Clay Holmes (6-8) went 5 1/3 innings for the Cubs and allowed six runs.
Eugenio Suárez tied it at 4 with a base hit to drive in Elly De La Cruz. Héctor Rodríguez grounded into a fielder's choice as Tyler Stephenson was called out at home before Trevino came through with the go-ahead hit.
De La Cruz also drove in two runs for the Reds, who dropped three of four to the Los Angeles Dodgers in their previous series.
Ian Happ homered in the third to tie it at 2 and Seiya Suzuki had a two-run single with the bases loaded in the fourth to put the Cubs up 4-3.
Julian Aguiar (2-1) got the win in relief, allowing two runs in three innings. All-Star starter Chase Burns, who is on an innings restriction, gave up two runs in three innings.
A matchup of left-handers on Saturday. Matthew Boyd (8-5, 4.16 ERA) takes the mound for Chicago while Nick Lodolo (3-5, 5.12) goes for Cincinnati.
___
This story has been corrected to show that Trevino’s two-run single came in the sixth inning, not the seventh.
___

item.title: [Akron Beacon Journal] As Guardians chase playoff spot, Jose Ramirez records career RBI 1,000
item.dc:creator: Ryan Lewis
item.description: As Guardians chase playoff spot, Jose Ramirez records career RBI 1,000 CLEVELAND — Cleveland’s baseball franchise has never had a player quite like Jose Ramirez. Along with signing under-market contracts to remain with the Guardians twice and the many memorable moments in a Cleveland uniform over the past decade-plus, his assault on the record books added another chapter Sept. 18 in a 5-3 win over the Athletics, which allowed them to retake the lead in the American League Central race with eight
item.content:encoded:
As Guardians chase playoff spot, Jose Ramirez records career RBI 1,000
CLEVELAND — Cleveland’s baseball franchise has never had a player quite like Jose Ramirez.
Along with signing under-market contracts to remain with the Guardians twice and the many memorable moments in a Cleveland uniform over the past decade-plus, his assault on the record books added another chapter Sept. 18 in a 5-3 win over the Athletics, which allowed them to retake the lead in the American League Central race with eight game remaining.
In that win, Ramirez went 2-for-5 with a home run and two RBIs, which gave him 1,000 RBIs in his career. In doing so, he became the 12th active player to reach 1,000 RBIs, joining Freddie Freeman, Paul Goldschmidt, Manny Machado, Giancarlo Stanton, Mike Trout, Bryce Harper, Nolan Arenado, Andrew McCutchen, Salvador Perez, Eugenio Suarez and Carlos Santana.
“Very important to thank God for that opportunity to play here in this organization and to be bale to achieve that,” Ramirez said through a team translator. “But the most important part is that we’re able to win today because you guys know what I really want to do here, which is win.”
Jose Ramirez stats
He’s also just the second Cleveland player to hit that milestone with the franchise, joining Earl Averill (1,084), whose playing career ended in the early 1940s.
It’s a significant line on Ramirez's Hall of Fame resume. The home run also brought him within three of becoming only the ninth player in MLB history to reach the 300/300 club for home runs and stolen bases.
“I like to use round numbers,” Guardians manager Stephen Vogt said. “It’s 10 years of 100 RBIs. When you break it down that way, it’s incredible what he has accomplished, and he’s not even close to being done. And very few people get do it, and it’s really cool to be here to watch it.”
It was a milestone night for Ramirez, though it came at the end of what has been one of his more frustrating seasons, particularly over the last few weeks while he’s played through hamate been surgery rehab.
Jose Ramirez injury update
He’s posted a 90 wRC+, which would be the first time since he became a full-time player in 2016 he’s been below 100 (league average). Since he returned to the lineup on July 22, after the procedure, he’s hit .216 with a .567 OPS.
“I keep working on it every day,” Ramirez said. “I have to keep working in the training room every day because this type of injury is the type where one day you feel good, the next you don’t feel so well, but you have to keep grinding.”
Despite the lack of his usual MVP-caliber production on a nightly basis, Vogt and the Guardians have still applauded the way Ramirez has fought through the situation. It’s one of the attributes that often gets mentioned first when listing why they feel he’s so valuable to the organization.
“Even as he was coming back and we have to give him off days, he was not happy about it,” Vogt said. “He wants to play every day. He wants to give us everything that he has on any given day. We know that there’s days where he’s not feeling good and he still goes out and gives 100 percent of what he has that day.
“It’s such a great example for our young guys to see that just because you’re not feeling 100 percent, it doesn’t mean you can’t go out and compete and contribute to help the team win.”
Ryan Lewis covers the Guardians for the Beacon Journal. He can be reached at rlewis1@gannett.com.

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Junior Caminero’s Success at the Plate Comes Thanks to One Key Metric
item.dc:creator: Julia Ruocchio; Unknown
item.description: For the second straight year, Tampa Bay Rays’ Junior Caminero has proven that he’s one of the game’s most talented hitters. He’s played two full seasons in the Big Leagues and has hit 40+ home runs in each of those seasons. At just 23 years old, Caminero continues to show the league day in and day out that he’s one of the most exciting young phenoms in the league. Not only is he making a case for himself as an American League MVP candidate, but he’s having all this success on one of the best tea
item.content:encoded:
For the second straight year, Tampa Bay Rays’ Junior Caminero has proven that he’s one of the game’s most talented hitters. He’s played two full seasons in the Big Leagues and has hit 40+ home runs in each of those seasons.
At just 23 years old, Caminero continues to show the league day in and day out that he’s one of the most exciting young phenoms in the league. Not only is he making a case for himself as an American League MVP candidate, but he’s having all this success on one of the best teams in the league. The Rays have the best record in the AL and have 93 wins.
A key reason for the immense success he’s had, particularly this past season, is his elite bat speed. Pair that with all of the other attributes he brings to the table, including his plate discipline, strength, quick hands, natural ability and his ability to adjust quickly, and Caminero’s future is as bright as anyone’s in the league.
Caminero’s average bat speed this season is 79.6 mph, the top mark among all 202 qualified hitters in the entire league, according to Statcast. For context as to how good this really is, the average bat speed for players in the league is about 72 mph.
Swing speed is key to Junior Caminero's success
“It’s his bat speed,” Tampa Bay’s manager Kevin Cash said. “I don’t know if anybody swings harder, quicker, whatever you want to do, in baseball.”
Cash added: “So it allows him to muscle through pitches. … He’s not squaring every single ball up. It’s just that he’s so quick getting the barrel through the zone. And it’s level enough to where he can cover a lot of different pitches at different angles. It’s not in and out of the zone."
When it comes to specific studies of his swing, Caminero’s flat, level swing is also a primary factor in his success. His swing has a vertical tilt of 25 degrees, according to Statcast. There are only four players in the league who have flatter swings than Caminero, as his swing ranks fifth in all of baseball in terms of angle and levelness.
Caminero spoke about how elite his numbers are and how he’s been able to achieve such incredible marks with stats including bat speed, bat angle and swing length, which is the longest in the league at 8.7 feet.
“God-given ability,” Caminero said. “God blessed me. I mean, thank God for this. We used to pray for this.”
He added: “It’s cool, because when somebody tells you that you have the fastest swing in the league, I say, ‘Wow!’ “When you see Aaron Judge, when you see Giancarlo Stanton, when you see Vladimir Guerrero (Jr.), you see Oneil Cruz, it’s the best, to be honest, to be within this group.”
Caminero’s teammate Drew Rasmussen spoke about the rare ability and talent that Caminero possesses.
“It’s unbelievable what he can do,” Rasmussen said. “It’s unbelievable how young he is, the maturity level that he possesses and his understanding and just how he’s grown into being a really, really good Major League Baseball player at the age of 23.”
Rasmussen revealed how he’d plan to pitch to Caminero if he were to face him.
“If we had to face him, I think I’d throw him four sliders in the left-handed batter’s box and hope he swings,” Rasmussen said. “And if he takes, he gets to go to first base. I mean, it’s better than giving up a homer.”
“It’s incredible,” Rasmussen added. “It’s just one of those things that every swing, regardless of pitch location, has the opportunity to (do) damage.”
Caminero’s stellar bat speed, as well as his swing level, are the core reasons for his abundance of success over the past two years for the Rays. He will look to continue that success in the regular season’s final weeks and into the postseason, as Tampa Bay makes its first postseason appearance since 2023.

item.title: [El Imparcial] MLB: Andrés Muñoz enfría intento de remontada con espectacular pickoff y consigue su salvamento 28 en 2026
item.dc:creator: Patrizio Caro
item.description: MLB: Andrés Muñoz enfría intento de remontada con espectacular pickoff y consigue su salvamento 28 en 2026 El cerrador mexicano protegió una ventaja mínima de Seattle ante Colorado, sorprendió a Cole Carrigg cuando amenazaba desde segunda base y terminó el juego con dos ponches para conseguir su rescate número 28 de la temporada. Andrés Muñoz volvió a cerrar la puerta para los Seattle Mariners, pero esta vez no necesitó únicamente de su poderosa recta para hacerlo. El mexicano realizó una jugada
item.content:encoded:
MLB: Andrés Muñoz enfría intento de remontada con espectacular pickoff y consigue su salvamento 28 en 2026
El cerrador mexicano protegió una ventaja mínima de Seattle ante Colorado, sorprendió a Cole Carrigg cuando amenazaba desde segunda base y terminó el juego con dos ponches para conseguir su rescate número 28 de la temporada.
Andrés Muñoz volvió a cerrar la puerta para los Seattle Mariners, pero esta vez no necesitó únicamente de su poderosa recta para hacerlo. El mexicano realizó una jugada defensiva clave en la novena entrada para frenar el intento de remontada de los Colorado Rockies y asegurar la victoria de Seattle por 5-4 este viernes 18 de septiembre en el Coors Field.
El sinaloense consiguió así su salvamento número 28 de la temporada 2026, luego de trabajar una entrada sin permitir carrera y recetar dos ponches. MLB confirmó al mexicano como el pitcher del salvamento tras el cerrado triunfo de los Mariners.
La entrada, sin embargo, estuvo lejos de ser tranquila.
¿Cómo fue el espectacular pickoff de Andrés Muñoz?
Seattle llegó a la parte baja de la novena con ventaja de apenas 5-4, después de que el joven Lázaro Montes rompiera el empate con un cuadrangular de 426 pies para abrir el episodio.
Muñoz entró entonces para proteger la diferencia mínima, pero Cole Carrigg abrió con sencillo y posteriormente se robó la segunda base, colocando inmediatamente la potencial carrera del empate en posición de anotar.
El mexicano respondió ponchando a Kyle Karros para conseguir el primer out.
Carrigg seguía representando una enorme amenaza desde segunda, pero su agresividad en los senderos terminó convirtiéndose en la oportunidad que necesitaba Muñoz.
El cerrador de Seattle sorprendió al corredor cuando intentaba avanzar rumbo a tercera base, consiguiendo el segundo out mediante el pickoff y eliminando de golpe al hombre que podía empatar el encuentro.
Con las bases nuevamente vacías, Muñoz atacó a Mickey Moniak y lo ponchó para poner punto final al encuentro.
Andrés Muñoz llega a 28 salvamentos en 2026
La actuación representó el rescate número 28 de Muñoz esta temporada y llegó después de una jornada en la que Colorado había conectado 15 imparables, pero dejó a 12 corredores en las bases.
Muñoz necesitó enfrentar una de las situaciones de mayor presión del partido y terminó la novena entrada sin carrera y con dos chocolates. En sus últimas siete apariciones registra cuatro salvamentos y ocho ponches en 6.2 entradas.
El triunfo dejó a Seattle con marca de 72-82. Aunque su panorama de postemporada es extremadamente complicado, los Mariners todavía se encontraban matemáticamente a seis juegos del último comodín de la Liga Americana con ocho partidos por disputar al concluir la jornada.
Te podría interesar: La regla de MLB que dejará al mexicano José Urquidy fuera de Playoffs con Phillies pese a urgencia en su rotación
Muñoz sigue escalando en la historia de Mariners
El salvamento también permite que el mexicano continúe acercándose a los máximos cerradores en la historia de Seattle.
El pasado 6 de septiembre, Muñoz consiguió su salvamento número 102 con los Mariners, superó los 101 de J.J. Putz y se colocó en el tercer lugar histórico de la franquicia. En aquel momento acumulaba 25 rescates durante la temporada.
Desde entonces sumó tres más, por lo que ahora alcanza 105 salvamentos con Seattle.
La lista histórica queda:
- Kazuhiro Sasaki: 129
- Edwin Díaz: 109
- Andrés Muñoz: 105
- J.J. Putz: 101
Esto significa que el sinaloense se encuentra a solamente cuatro salvamentos de empatar a Edwin Díaz en el segundo puesto y a cinco de superarlo.
Muñoz también es ya el tercer pitcher nacido en México con más de 100 salvamentos en Grandes Ligas, únicamente detrás de Joakim Soria y Roberto Osuna.
Su rescate número 28 quizá no llegó únicamente con el espectáculo habitual de lanzamientos cercanos a las 100 millas por hora. Esta vez, una rápida lectura del corredor y un pickoff en el momento de mayor peligro terminaron siendo las armas con las que Andrés Muñoz apagó el último intento de remontada de Colorado.

이정후는 2회초 첫 타석에서 솔로 홈런을 때려냈다.
샌프란시스코가 0-1로 끌려가던 2회초 선두타자로 타석에 들어선 이정후는 다저스 우완 선발 투수 타일러 글래스노우를 상대로 오른쪽 담장을 넘기는 동점 솔로 홈런을 쏘아올렸다.
이정후는 볼카운트 2볼-2스트라이크에서 스트라이크존 한복판에 몰린 5구째 너클커브를 노려쳤다. 타구는 시속 97.7마일(약 157.2㎞)의 속도로 날아가 우측 펜스를 넘어갔다.
8월 11일 휴스턴 애스트로스전 이후 39일 만에 손맛을 본 이정후는 시즌 10홈런을 채웠다.
다만 이어진 타석에서 안타를 추가하진 못했다.
팀이 2-1 역전에 성공한 3회초 2사 1, 2루 달아날 찬스에 다시 나선 이정후는 중견수 뜬공으로 물러나며 이닝을 매듭지었다. 양 팀이 다시 2-2 균형을 맞춘 6회초 1사 2루엔 우익수 뜬공을 쳐 진루타를 만드는 데 만족해야 했다.
샌프란시스코가 8회에만 홈런 무려 4방을 맞고 2-8까지 밀린 뒤 이정후는 9회초 선두타자로 다시 나섰으나 3루수 파울플라이로 아웃됐다.
2024년 빅리그에 데뷔한 이정후가 한 시즌에 두 자릿수 홈런을 친 것은 올 시즌이 처음이다. 지난해 8개가 개인 한 시즌 최다 홈런이었다.
이미 12도루를 기록 중이던 이정후는 MLB 10홈런-10도루도 달성했다.
지난 17일 세인트루이스 카디널스전에서 4타수 무안타에 그쳤던 이정후는 이날 홈런으로 아쉬움을 털어냈다.
안타 없이 홈런만 1개를 기록한 이정후의 시즌 타율은 0.274를 유지했다.
한편 이미 내셔널리그 서부지구 1위를 확정한 다저스는 8회에만 맥스 먼시, 카일 터커, 무키 베츠, 윌 스미스의 홈런포가 연달아 터지며 8-2 승리를 거뒀다. 시즌94승(60패)째다.
반면 내셔널리그 서부지구 4위 샌프란시스코는 시즌 90패(64승)째를 당했다.

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Zac Gallen Makes First Career Bullpen Appearance in Brutal Yankees Blowout
item.dc:creator: Alex D'Agostino; Unknown
item.description: For the first time in his eight-year major league career, Arizona Diamondbacks right-hander Zac Gallen found himself trotting out of the bullpen and taking the mound in the seventh inning. item.content:encoded:
For the first time in his eight-year major league career, Arizona Diamondbacks right-hander Zac Gallen found himself trotting out of the bullpen and taking the mound in the seventh inning. He had never once pitched in relief in MLB — even following an opener.
Gallen, after a brutal start to his 2026 season and a multi-month layoff due to elbow inflammation, was moved to a bullpen role following an unsuccessful return debut.
That decision was officially announced on September 13, and it took five days for him to make his first relief outing.
Unfortunately for Gallen and the Diamondbacks, it came in a game that already looked bleak. The hard-hitting New York Yankees had already pummeled starter Eduardo Rodriguez for six runs in 5.1 innings. Arizona trailed 7-2 when Gallen took the mound.
How Zac Gallen performed in first bullpen appearance
Gallen pitched the final three innings of Friday night's game, allowing two runs in the process. Only one was earned, due to a throwing error by first baseman Pavin Smith on a ground ball that should have been an out. He threw 68 pitches, 41 of them landing for strikes.
The issue? Gallen allowed two base hits and walked two batters in the proces. His velocity was up a touch on his slider, which was his most primarily-used offering. He was able to pick up four whiffs on 12 swings with that pitch.
His four-seam fastball, however, was once again close to nonexistent. Of those 68 pitches, only 10 were four-seams. He did not manage to pick up a whiff on six swings, and was only able to land two of them in the zone for called strikes.
It's not exactly an encouraging or discouraging sign to see Gallen perform this way in a relief capacity. He did not showcase elite-level improvement with his velocity or movement, and he struggled with base traffic, as well as putting away batters. His ERA went down, but only to 6.12 on the year.
Unfortunately, even if Gallen had pitched three elite innings, the Diamondbacks would not have had much of a chance to engineer a victory. Trailing by five runs before they even came up to bat, Arizona never closed the deficit to lower than four runs on the night. They lost 9-2.
With the San Diego Padres taking down the Miami Marlins, 8-2, Arizona now sits five games back of the third and final Wild Card berth, with just eight games left on the schedule. Time is quickly running out.
An Arizona native, Alex D'Agostino is the Publisher and credentialed reporter for Arizona Diamondbacks On SI. He previously served as Deputy Editor for Arizona Diamondbacks and Arizona Cardinals On SI and covered both teams for FanSided. Alex also writes for PHNX Sports. Follow Alex on X/Twitter @AlexDagAZ.
Follow alexdagaz

While there are still eight games left to play -- and three against the Padres who Arizona trails in the race for the No. 3 National League Wild Card spot -- the Diamondbacks need to win games, and that's something that has eluded them of late. The loss was the third in a row for the Diamondbacks, who have dropped six of their past eight games. Arizona opened the night four games behind the Padres and five b
item.content:encoded:
PHOENIX -- It feels like the Diamondbacks’ postseason hopes are slipping away from them.
While there are still eight games left to play -- and three against the Padres who Arizona trails in the race for the No. 3 National League Wild Card spot -- the Diamondbacks need to win games, and that's something that has eluded them of late.
The loss was the third in a row for the Diamondbacks, who have dropped six of their past eight games. Arizona opened the night four games behind the Padres and five behind the Cubs and Phillies, who are tied for the NL Wild Card lead.
This game never really seemed in doubt as the Yankees jumped on Eduardo Rodriguez in the first inning for five runs. The Bronx Bombers sent nine men to the plate in the inning and drew three walks, all of which scored, as Rodriguez threw a whopping 45 pitches in the inning.
The Diamondbacks did get a spark from Corbin Carroll, whose struggles of late prompted manager Torey Lovullo to drop him to seventh in the batting order. Carroll hit a two-run homer off Gerrit Cole in the second, but it was not nearly enough.

item.title: [MLB.com] Garcia's clutch hit vs. reigning Cy Young winner a bright spot in tough 2026
item.dc:creator: John Perrotto
item.description: Garcia is thankful to be back in the starting lineup for the final days of the 2026 regular season. He has been limited to just 76 games, because of a partial tear of his left hamstring and just returned from the injured list on Tuesday after missing 21 games. “I didn’t think I might play again this year, so I’m thankful,” Garcia said following Friday night’s 8-5 loss to the Pirates to open a three-game series at PNC Park. “I just wish there were more games left.” Garcia had high hopes for 2026
item.content:encoded:
Garcia is thankful to be back in the starting lineup for the final days of the 2026 regular season. He has been limited to just 76 games, because of a partial tear of his left hamstring and just returned from the injured list on Tuesday after missing 21 games.
“I didn’t think I might play again this year, so I’m thankful,” Garcia said following Friday night’s 8-5 loss to the Pirates to open a three-game series at PNC Park. “I just wish there were more games left.”
Garcia had high hopes for 2026 after making his first All-Star Game appearance last season, then signing a five-year, $57.5 million contract extension that runs through 2030 and includes a club option for ‘31.
Alas, Garcia is slashing .262/.318/.378 with three home runs.
However, the 26-year-old provided a bright spot against Pittsburgh in what turned out to be a frustrating night for Kansas City. Garcia’s two-run double in the third inning helped the Royals build a 4-0 lead against reigning National League Cy Young winner Paul Skenes.
Still, they eventually lost for the 12th time in their last 17 games despite home runs by Vinnie Pasquantino and Michael Massey.
“We think the world of Mikey,” manager Matt Quatraro said of Garcia. “We committed a lot of years and a lot of money to him, because we think he’s a really good player who can help us win. Getting him back on the field is important for us, and it’s good for him, too.
“He probably thought his season was over, but he worked very hard through the rehab process to get back. And he got a big hit in a big spot.”
Just eight games remain for the Royals, so there isn’t a whole lot of season left to salvage for Garcia. Yet, he appreciates what few days remain and getting a big hit off a Cy Young winner.
“I like to face the best pitchers,” Garcia said with a smile. “It makes me fight that much harder. It felt really good to get a big hit there with a couple of guys on base. It’s been a tough year for me personally, but we have come back here, we want to finish the season healthy, and we want to help the team win some games. I want to go home for the winter with a good feeling.”
The usually unflappable Randy Dobnak admittedly was fighting some feelings when he took the mound in his hometown for just the second time in his career. The right-hander grew up in suburban South Park, Pa.
Dobnak’s previous appearance at PNC Park came with the Twins in 2020. However, fans weren’t permitted to attend games during that pandemic-shortened season. Dobnak estimated he had at least 200 family members and friends in the stands and had attended approximately 300 games in this ballpark.
“This was really kind of special,” Dobnak said. “After I threw my last warm-up pitch, I stood there on the mound and took it all in. Growing up, this was the place I always wanted to be. I caught myself almost getting a little bit emotional out there.”
Dobnak paused and chuckled.
“That quickly changed when I threw my first pitch and [Konnor] Griffin singled right back up the middle,” he said.
Unfortunately for Dobnak and his throng of supporters, that signaled what was to come. He lasted just 3 2/3 innings and gave up four runs on seven hits and two walks, while striking out one.
Dobnak left with a 5-3 lead, but the Pirates rallied against the Royals’ bullpen. Spencer Horwitz’s two-run single off Nate Pearson in a three-run seventh inning broke a 5-5 tie.
“I think the biggest thing was first-pitch strikes with Randy,” Quatraro said. “It was an interesting game for him. There were four hits down the third-base line from a left-handed hitter and a couple of infield hits. He had a lot of traffic to deal with.”

item.title: [Toronto Star] Blue Jays vs. Rangers: Dylan Cease and Toronto’s fading wild-card hopes hit the wall in Texas
item.dc:creator: Gregor Chisholm

item.content:encoded:
Dylan Cease appears to have run out of gas, and the same could be said about the Blue Jays’ ability to make the playoffs.
Cease has been carrying the starting rotation and middling offence for most of the year. The heavy lifting clearly took a toll for the stretch run.
The velocity on Cease’s fastball has been steadily declining for several weeks and dipped even lower in a 7-1 road loss to the Texas Rangers on Friday night. The 30-year-old right-hander allowed four runs and couldn’t get out of the third inning of the pivotal series opener.
Meanwhile, the Cleveland Guardians won to move into first place in the American League Central, while the Chicago White Sox lost. That means the Jays trail the White Sox by two games for the final wild-card spot, and they do not own the tiebreaker.
Cease’s poor showing should also eliminate him from Cy Young consideration. That honour will likely go to Yankees right-hander Cam Schlittler, who has pitched more innings (184 2/3 vs. 169) with a lower ERA (1.95 vs. 2.40) and fewer walks/hits per inning pitched (0.90 vs. 1.10).
It wasn’t supposed to end this way. Through the first five months, Cease was consistently hitting the upper-90s in miles per hour with his fastball. That high velocity combined with a wipeout slider turned him into the major-league leader in strikeouts and a front-runner to win the first Cy Young of his career.
The warning signs started earlier this month. Against the Athletics on Sept. 7, his average fastball velocity fell below 95 m.p.h. for the first time since 2023. The problems continued in Cease’s next outing versus the Baltimore Orioles, when he failed to average 95 m.p.h. or higher in back-to-back starts for the first time in the big leagues.
The lack of heat became an even bigger issue in Texas. Through the first couple of innings, his fastball sat in the 91-to-93-m.p.h. range. By the time he walked off the field with his team trailing by four, his average was still only 93.6 m.p.h., a career low.
The other issue against Texas was that his command was all over the place. Cease threw just 36 of 74 pitches for strikes with an alarming six walks, his most since Aug. 16 of last year.
Every inning, every pitch was a grind. Cease walked two in the first inning, but escaped unscathed. There were two more walks and a single by Nicky López in the second to load the bases.
The turning point came on the next ground ball when shortstop Ernie Clement made an ill-advised throw to third base. He was trying to get the force out, but his throw bounced off Jake Burger’s helmet and ricocheted down the line as two runners scored.
Cease then served up a sacrifice fly to Ezequiel Durán before Corey Seager added an RBI double and the Rangers jumped in front 4-0. Cease returned for the third, but loaded the bases again before he was replaced by Brendan Cellucci.
The late-season swoon will likely teach the Jays some valuable lessons about how to handle Cease in the future. On the surface, 169 innings is a reasonable workload. But this isn’t about how many outs he recorded, it’s about how many pitches he threw while doing it.
There were four consecutive starts in April and May when Cease threw at least 106 pitches, followed by seven straight starts of at least 102 in June and July, including a season-high 120. There was another stretch of four starts with 100-plus pitches in August.
The Jays continue to insist Cease is fine and there are no injury concerns. That’s probably true — if not, it would be a fireable offence — but it doesn’t change the fact that he has clearly worn down and no longer resembles the pitcher he was through the first five months.
The bigger issue is that the loss was a major blow to the lethargic Jays’ playoff hopes. They have eight games left to make up three games in the standings; Toronto owns the tiebreaker with the Guardians, but not with the White Sox.
After playing mediocre baseball through the first four months, the Jays had little margin for error in August and September. They needed to be at their best over the last couple of weeks and instead were at their worst.
The season isn’t technically over, but a 4-7 stretch has put them on the brink. Their only shot now is winning almost all of their remaining games while hoping for a total collapse by the White Sox.

item.content:encoded:
Ronald Acuña Jr. blasted a two-run homer on Friday, leading the Braves to a 6-2 win over the Astros.

Acuña helped Atlanta secure a playoff spot for the eighth time in the last nine years when he blasted a no-doubter to left field off Astros workhorse reliever AJ Blubaugh in the seventh inning. It was his sixth round-tripper in 16 games since the outset of September. The 28-year-old fantasy superstar is just one home run shy of posting a 20-homer, 20-steal campaign for the first time since his historic 41-homer, 73-steal effort back in 2023. He may never reach those lofty heights again, but he’s proven he can be an impactful power/speed combo threat, even if he doesn’t come close to playing a full season ever again.

He last accomplished the feat back in 2023 when he launched a whopping 54 big flies in his second season with Atlanta.
